This paper investigates passive control for drag reduction on a simplified road vehicle geometry, specifically the square-back Windsor body, through the optimization of a rear roof extension. The study employs high-fidelity wall-resolved large eddy simulation (LES) to model the flow. The optimization process relies on Gaussian process-based surrogate modeling combined with Bayesian optimization, guided by an expected improvement criterion, to efficiently explore the design space defined by the roof extension’s taper penetration distance, angle of incidence, and length.
The optimization converged within six iterations, requiring a total of 60 LES simulations, and resulted in a 6.5% reduction in drag. The authors identified six distinct mechanisms contributing to this drag reduction, including diffuser-induced pressure recovery, base-size reduction, and modifications to the vertical wake balance. The optimal configuration was found when the roof extension angle corresponded to the onset of separation, with both the taper penetration distance and extension length at their maximum values within the analyzed domain.
This work provides a framework for aerodynamic optimization, demonstrating how coupled wake–geometry interactions can be effectively managed for improved aerodynamic performance. While the application is to road vehicles, the methodology of using Gaussian processes for design optimization with high-fidelity CFD is relevant to broader engineering design challenges.

Type: 🤖 ML/Heating Prediction | Relevance: 88/100
Duan and colleagues introduce an augmented data fusion framework aimed at predicting aerodynamic heating on hypersonic vehicles. This framework combines data enhancement strategies with a multifidelity U-NET (MF-UNet) architecture. The approach addresses the challenges of sparse experimental data and the inherent trade-offs in accuracy and resolution associated with traditional CFD and wind-tunnel measurements. The MF-UNet is developed to optimize multifidelity mapping for high-precision heat-flux reconstruction, while systematic data augmentation expands limited experimental datasets to improve extrapolation capabilities.
The methodology was validated on a hypersonic double-ellipsoid configuration. It successfully integrated three sparse experimental datasets to generate complete surface heating profiles. The framework demonstrated significant improvements over baseline CFD solutions, achieving a surface-averaged normalized root-mean-square error below 3% when compared with experimental measurements. The approach enables full-surface extrapolation, even with limited experimental inputs.
This work provides a practical solution for aerodynamic heating analysis by effectively integrating multifidelity data, particularly sparse experimental measurements, with a deep learning model. The ability to generate complete heating profiles and extrapolate to new conditions from limited experimental data is valuable for design cycles where experimental campaigns are costly and time-consuming.

Type: 💻 Numerical/CFD | Relevance: 68/100
This paper investigates the influence of pilot hot gas injection on flame stabilization within a cavity-based scramjet combustor. The authors employed three-dimensional unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations to model ethylene fuel injection in a dual-solution regime, where two distinct flame stabilization modes could exist. The primary goal was to understand how pilot injection, at varying heating levels, affects both ignition and sustained flame stabilization, particularly focusing on potential mode transitions.
The simulations revealed that flame stabilization is highly sensitive to the pilot heating power. A low level of pilot heating maintained the flame in a cavity shear-layer stabilization mode. However, when the pilot heating was sufficiently high, it induced a transition to a jet-wake stabilization mode. This transition was primarily attributed to a reduction in the ignition delay within the unburned jet-wake region, caused by the elevated temperatures from the pilot. Additionally, pilot injection was found to enhance fuel–air mixing through the generation of vortices, with both the reduced ignition delay and mixing enhancement intensifying as the pilot heating power increased. Consequently, high heating power facilitated upstream flame propagation and flow separation, which ultimately triggered the observed mode transition. A theoretical analysis, based on Semenov thermal ignition theory, supported these findings by showing that high pilot heating promoted chemical heat release in the unburned jet-wake, exceeding the enthalpy outflow of the initial cavity shear-layer mode, leading to a sustained temperature rise and initiating the transition.
Understanding these flame stabilization mode transitions is important for the design and operation of scramjet engines. The ability to control or predict such transitions through pilot injection strategies directly impacts the reliability and performance envelope of high-speed propulsion systems, which are critical for applications like high-speed missiles.

Type: 💻 Numerical/CFD | Relevance: 75/100
This paper investigates the impact of vibration–vibration–translation (VVT) reactions in state-to-state (StS) simulations of high-enthalpy nitrogen flow over a sphere. The primary objective is to reduce the significant computational cost associated with detailed StS simulations by evaluating two simplification methods: multiquantum restrictions and simplifying VVT transitions to vibration–translation (VTm) transitions. This work extends a previous study, systematically analyzing how these transition models affect flowfield characteristics and, crucially, heat flux distributions.
The numerical results demonstrate that both the full StS VVT model and the simplified VTm model predict nearly identical shock standoff distances and stagnation-point heat fluxes. These predictions align well with available experimental data. When comparing VVT and VTm transitions, the study finds minimal differences in the predictions of translational temperature, vibrational temperature, and nitrogen mass fraction. Near the wall, both models yield almost identical state populations, which exhibit gradually pronounced non-Boltzmann distributions.
The key finding is that VVT transitions can be effectively reduced to VTm transitions without compromising essential accuracy for predicting aerodynamic heating in this high-enthalpy nitrogen flow scenario. This outcome is valuable for the aerothermodynamics community, as it offers a practical approach to decrease the computational burden of detailed state-to-state simulations, making them more feasible for multidimensional applications while maintaining accuracy in critical heating predictions.

Type: 💻 Numerical/CFD | Relevance: 75/100
This paper presents a comparative analysis of several boundary-layer stability codes applied to hypersonic, high-enthalpy flows over blunted cones. The study focuses on two geometries: a 7-degree and a 10.9-degree half-angle blunted cone. The primary objective is to assess the influence of different numerical approaches on second-mode instability and to characterize the role of high-temperature gas effects. The computational results from seven distinct stability codes are compared against experimental data obtained from the High Enthalpy Shock Tunnel (HIEST) in Japan and the High-Enthalpy Laboratory Munich (HELM) in Germany.
The analysis quantifies the impact of high-temperature gas effects on the second mode and investigates the influence of uncertainties, such as minor variations in mean-flow conditions or wall temperature. A specific comparison is also performed between air and CO2 test gases, highlighting differences in stability characteristics under varying gas compositions. The paper provides insights into the agreement and discrepancies among the various computational methods and their ability to reproduce experimental observations under high-enthalpy conditions.
This work is significant for the aerothermodynamics community as it enhances confidence in computational tools used for predicting boundary-layer stability and transition on high-speed vehicles. A better understanding of second-mode instability and real gas effects in high-enthalpy flows is crucial for accurate aerodynamic heating predictions and the design of effective thermal protection systems for hypersonic missiles and reentry vehicles.

Type: 💻 Numerical/CFD | Relevance: 65/100
This paper investigates the effectiveness of spanwise heterogeneous, ridge-type wall roughness in passively controlling shock-wave/turbulent boundary-layer interactions (STBLIs). The authors employed wall-resolved large-eddy simulations (LES) to analyze a Mach 2.0 impinging STBLI flow with a 40-degree impinging-shock angle. They considered incoming turbulent boundary layers at two friction Reynolds numbers, approximately 350 and 1200, and explored multiple roughness configurations scaled by either inner or outer flow parameters.
The results indicate that while the rough-wall configurations introduce a moderate increase in mean drag, they substantially alter the dynamics of the interaction. The wall-pressure fluctuations near the separation-shock foot, which consist of low-frequency components from large-scale shock excursions and high-frequency components from amplified turbulence, were significantly attenuated. At the lower Reynolds number, both low- and high-frequency components contributed comparably to the overall reduction. At the higher Reynolds number, a stronger overall reduction of the pressure fluctuation peak was observed, primarily due to the effective suppression of the low-frequency component. Cross-correlation analyses suggest downstream mechanisms drive the low-frequency dynamics in this strong interaction regime, where large-scale shock excursions are mainly driven by the breathing of the reverse-flow bubble. Large-scale Görtler-like vortices were identified around the reattachment location in all cases, appearing largely unaffected by roughness geometry.
This work provides valuable insights into passive flow control strategies for STBLIs, which are critical phenomena in high-speed flight. Understanding how wall roughness can modify turbulence and shock dynamics offers potential avenues for mitigating adverse effects in supersonic and hypersonic vehicle designs, particularly in areas prone to strong shock interactions.

Type: 💻 Numerical/CFD | Relevance: 75/100
This paper investigates how wall curvature influences the evolution of Mack modes in hypersonic boundary layers, a critical factor for boundary layer transition. The authors use linearized compressible Navier-Stokes equations to parametrically study flat-plate, concave, and convex curvatures, aiming to understand their impact on transition mechanisms. The work addresses a gap in understanding curvature effects on Mack modes in hypersonic flows, building upon existing research that primarily focuses on freestream parameters.
The study’s findings indicate that convex curvature stabilizes Mack modes due to favorable pressure gradients, while concave curvature destabilizes them through adverse pressure gradients. As curvature increases, these effects become more pronounced: greater convex curvature further suppresses Mack modes, and greater concave curvature amplifies them. The research provides a detailed numerical analysis of these physical phenomena.
Understanding these curvature effects is important for the design of hypersonic configurations, as boundary layer transition significantly affects aerodynamic heating and vehicle performance. The insights gained offer guidance for managing transition location, which is crucial for thermal management and overall vehicle integrity.

Type: 🤖 ML/Transition | Relevance: 85/100
This paper explores methods to enhance Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models for predicting boundary layer transition, specifically focusing on Tollmien-Schlichting (TS) instability waves in subsonic boundary layers. The authors aimed to improve the accuracy of ANNs in forecasting the amplification rates of these waves, which are fundamental to determining transition location. Their approach involved applying recent machine learning developments, including surrogate optimization techniques and strategic augmentation of the training data, to refine the ANN models.
The optimized ANN models, trained on the modified dataset, demonstrated a significant improvement in prediction accuracy. They reduced the average transition location errors on various airfoils and flow conditions by 51% compared to the original manually-tuned network. These transition locations were benchmarked against results from the Langley Stability and Transition Analysis Code (LASTRAC).
This work contributes to making linear stability theory-based transition prediction more computationally efficient and less user-intensive for integration into computational fluid dynamics codes, particularly for general aviation applications where TS waves are the dominant transition mechanism.

Type: 🤖 ML/Aerodynamics | Relevance: 40/100
This paper describes a methodology for optimizing the design of a long-range Mars rotorcraft by integrating high-fidelity simulation data with machine learning techniques. The approach begins with generating extensive aerodynamic simulation databases for a hex-rotor bi-plane tailsitter aircraft across various geometric perturbations and flight conditions. Over 3,000 full aircraft aerodynamic simulations were performed using GPU-enabled OVERFLOW with an actuator disk model, taking approximately 1.5 weeks on 32 GPU nodes equipped with 128 NVIDIA V100 GPUs.
Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), sparse GPRs, and various Neural Networks were then trained as surrogate models to predict airfoil and airframe aerodynamic performance based on flight conditions, airframe geometry, and rotor control inputs. These surrogate models, combined with additional modules for aircraft mass and inertia, enabled another 3,000 aircraft simulations in CAMRAD-II in less than six hours using 240 CPU cores. This significantly reduced the computational cost for subsequent design iterations. The framework was then configured for simultaneous optimization of aircraft parameters and flight conditions, aiming for objectives such as maximum range or endurance while satisfying controllability constraints.
This work demonstrates a practical application of data-driven methods to bring higher-fidelity simulation data into the early stages of conceptual design. By creating accurate and efficient surrogate models, the design process can achieve improved accuracy and potentially identify critical design issues much earlier than traditional methods, despite the computational expense of the initial high-fidelity data generation.

This paper introduces a methodology for predicting the probability of obstacle collision for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) operating in windy conditions. The approach centers on using Gaussian Process Regression to create a fast, approximate representation of wind fields along a predefined trajectory. This wind model then feeds into a 6-degrees-of-freedom UAV trajectory simulator, which incorporates a rotorcraft lumped-mass model and an LQRI controller to simulate trajectory deviations. The study considers both steady-state wind and dynamic wind gust effects.
The authors demonstrate the method using real flight data from an octocopter at NASA Langley Research Center. They compute collision probabilities against simulated obstacles under various wind conditions. The work also explores the impact of varying wind conditions and UAV airspeeds, correlating these with experimental flights and data from ground-based weather stations.
The presented approach offers a way to quickly assess safety thresholds, such as minimum separation from obstacles or available battery resources, by accounting for wind-induced trajectory deviations. This capability supports risk-informed decision-making for managing safety-critical events in autonomous systems.

Type: 🤖 ML/Aerodynamics | Relevance: 85/100
This paper introduces Structured Covariance Gaussian Networks (SCGNs), a new method for nonlinear regression and uncertainty quantification. The approach involves a pair of neural networks that parameterize the mean and a dense covariance function of a multivariate Gaussian process. These networks are trained together to maximize the log-likelihood of the observed data, with the covariance matrix constructed to ensure positive definiteness at every input. The authors also present a sampling technique to generate viable surrogate function realizations from the Gaussian process, applying the SCGN model to learn an aerodynamic response surface with built-in uncertainty for the Orion crew module.
The results indicate that SCGN provides an efficient and systematic way to learn complex nonlinear functional relationships and dense covariances. When compared to a baseline Gaussian process regressor, SCGN delivers comparable uncertainty descriptions while demonstrating improved scalability with increasing dataset size. The sample functions produced by SCGN are quick to evaluate online, making them suitable for integration into trajectory simulations.
These findings suggest that SCGN is a viable computational method for aerodynamic uncertainty quantification. Its ability to combine the flexibility of neural networks with the uncertainty quantification capabilities of Gaussian processes, particularly with improved scalability, holds promise for the design and analysis of high-speed vehicles where accurate aerodynamic predictions and their associated uncertainties are critical.

Type: 🤖 ML/Aerodynamics | Relevance: 88/100
This paper addresses the critical need to incorporate model uncertainty when developing aerodynamic models from data, aiming to create probabilistic aerodynamic databases. It explores methods for sampling deterministic functions from two types of probabilistic models: Gaussian Process Regressors (GPRs) and a specific neural network architecture. A key challenge for GPRs is generating consistent function evaluations across multiple samples when input points are not predetermined.
For GPRs, the paper presents an approach to achieve consistent function sampling. For the neural network architecture, which learns a conditional Gaussian distribution by maximizing marginal likelihood, it discusses and compares various options for generating sample functions that align with this learned distribution. The utility of these probabilistic aerodynamic models is then demonstrated through an application in an atmospheric reentry simulation. The abstract does not provide specific quantitative results such as Mach numbers, RMSE values, or speedup factors from these demonstrations.
The work is significant for the aerothermodynamics community as it directly contributes to building more reliable aerodynamic models by quantifying and propagating uncertainty. This capability is essential for robust design, control, and trajectory planning of high-speed missiles and reentry vehicles, where accurate aerodynamic predictions under varying conditions are paramount.

What is AeroSentinel? AeroSentinel is an AI-powered research intelligence platform that tracks the latest developments in aerothermodynamics, hypersonic flow physics, and AI/ML applications in CFD.
Every week, the system scans 7 top-tier academic databases for new publications, filters them through a multi-layer quality gate, and publishes curated bilingual paper reviews – all driven by a Telegram bot with one-tap approval.
Research Focus The platform tracks research across three main areas:
Aerodynamic heating – prediction, measurement, and simulation of surface heat flux on high-speed vehicles AI/ML surrogates for CFD – Gaussian process regression, neural networks, deep learning, and physics-informed methods applied to aerodynamic and aerothermodynamic problems Hypersonic flow physics – boundary layer transition, shock-boundary layer interaction, real gas effects, stagnation point heating Each paper gets its own individual review post with readable prose summaries, a type badge, and a relevance score.
Sources Papers are sourced from 7 academic databases:
OpenAlex – broad academic coverage (200M+ works), with journal tier and institution filtering Crossref – 70M+ articles, DOI-based metadata, with thesis/dissertation discovery CORE – 200M+ open access articles, including theses and grey literature Semantic Scholar – citation velocity, influential citation counts, abstract enrichment arXiv – latest preprints, restricted to physics and computational categories with aerospace topic relevance check NASA NTRS – NASA technical reports and memoranda (always Tier 1) IEEE Xplore – IEEE conference and journal papers (optional, requires API key) Quality System Journal Tiers Tier 1 (always kept): AIAA Journal, Journal of Fluid Mechanics, Physics of Fluids, Journal of Spacecraft and Rockets, Aerospace Science and Technology, Shock Waves, and others Tier 2 (kept with citation velocity or elite institution): Computers & Fluids, Acta Astronautica, International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer, Chinese Journal of Aeronautics, and others Tier 0 (blocked, except theses/dissertations): unranked journals Scoring Papers are scored (0-100+) based on journal tier, source, keyword priority match, citation metrics, recency, and abstract availability. Only papers scoring 30+ are included.
Thesis Discovery Crossref dissertations and CORE theses bypass the tier-0 filter, enabling discovery of relevant PhD and MSc work. These still pass through scoring, so irrelevant theses are naturally filtered out.
AI Analysis Each paper review is generated by Gemini 2.5 Flash and includes:
Natural prose summaries – 2-3 paragraphs written like a knowledgeable colleague explaining the paper, not a structured checklist 9 paper type classifications – ML/Heating, ML/Aerodynamics, ML/Transition, Numerical/CFD, Experimental, Analytical, Review, Multi-Method, Thesis 36 curated tags – Strict English-only vocabulary covering research domains, methodologies, physical phenomena, flow regimes, applications, and cross-cutting topics Relevance scoring (0-100) based on proximity to the research focus areas Anti-slop filter – 24 banned AI filler phrases blocked in prompts and scrubbed from output Bilingual output – Every review in both English and Turkish Telegram Bot Control everything from Telegram:
Command Description /scout Trigger a paper hunt now /search Interactive custom search – pick from 36 tags, set date range /bibtex Export latest digest as BibTeX citations /bookmarks View your bookmarked digests /status Check latest workflow status /help Show available commands Draft previews arrive with one-tap Publish / Edit / Discard / Bookmark buttons.
Technical Details Fully automated – GitHub Actions runs the pipeline on schedule (weekly) or on demand via Telegram Open source – github.com/sezersivri/aerosentinel $0/month – GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Worker, Gemini API, Telegram Bot API, and all academic APIs are free tier Privacy first – No analytics, no tracking, no cookies Built with Hugo (PaperMod theme), Python 3.11, Cloudflare Workers, Gemini 2.5 Flash Current version: 2.5.0
